scams.name: Nanjing Road Tea House / Bar Scam
scams.description:
You are walking along Nanjing Road's pedestrian strip when two young Chinese visitors strike up conversation in fluent English — they are visiting from Xi'an, also seeing Shanghai for the first time, and keen to share a traditional tea ceremony nearby. The setup is warm and unhurried. The venue they suggest is just a few minutes away on a side street off Tianjin Road, and it looks the part once you arrive: low lighting, wooden furniture, ceramic cups.

The tea is served and the atmosphere feels authentic. Then the bill arrives: ¥3,000, ¥6,000, ¥10,000. The two visitors who brought you in are no longer at the table. Staff explain the rate per cup, per pot, per ceremony fee, and the total bears no relationship to anything you expected. When you resist, the door locks or staff position themselves at the exit. Payment in cash or Alipay is demanded; credit-card chargeback is often the only recovery route once you are outside.

Any stranger who approaches you on Nanjing Road, near People's Square, or along the Bund and steers you toward a "nearby" tea ceremony in fluent English is running this scam — the friendliness is the technique. Say "bu yao xie xie" and keep walking without breaking stride. For legitimate Shanghai tea, the Huxinting Teahouse at Yu Garden has served at posted prices of ¥150–¥300 since 1855; walk in directly rather than following anyone else's lead.
scams.avoidance: Walk past any stranger approaching near Nanjing Road with 'bu yao xie xie' Never follow a stranger to a 'nearby' tea house — the venue is always the scam Avoid 510 Tianjin Road (SMOOTH dining bar) and any similar side-street 'tea' venue For genuine tea, go to Shanghai Propaganda Poster Art Centre cafe or hotel-concierge-recommended venues If trapped, photograph the bill, pay with credit card (for chargeback leverage), then report to 12315 and your card company
scams.location: Nanjing Road East and West pedestrian shopping area, side streets off People's Square, Tianjin Road, Bund approach
scams.tldr: Two "friendly travelers" on Nanjing Road East pedestrian strip approach tourists with English conversation, steer them within minutes into a side-street tea house, then present a locked-door bill of ¥3,000–¥10,000 for a ceremony that costs under ¥300 at a legitimate venue.

scams.name: Pudong (PVG) Airport Black Taxi & Meter Rigging
scams.description:
You clear customs at Pudong International Airport and follow the signs toward the taxi stand. Before you reach the official queue, a man in casual clothes breaks from a group near the arrivals exit: "Taxi? Shanghai city? Good price, 400 yuan." He looks unhurried and speaks passable English. The legitimate metered fare from PVG to central Shanghai is ¥180–¥220 for the 45-kilometer ride to Nanjing Road or the Bund.

Going with the tout means paying double the meter rate — and you have no registered vehicle number, no receipt, and no recourse if the driver adds a luggage fee at the destination or takes a longer route. The scam density at the Longyang Road taxi rank (reached after taking the Maglev from PVG) is reportedly worse than at the airport itself. Licensed cabs with tampered meters running faster than the 3.2-yuan-per-kilometer base rate have also been documented in Shanghai in recent years.

Take Shanghai Metro Line 2 from PVG Pudong Airport station to People's Square for ¥7 — it is the only fully scam-proof route from arrivals , running every 6–10 minutes with direct connections in 90 minutes. If you need a car, install DiDi before flying and order from the official rideshare pickup zone; for a licensed street taxi, say "da biao" (打表 — "run the meter") before boarding and photograph the license plate from the rear windscreen before you move.
scams.avoidance: Take Shanghai Metro Line 2 from PVG station: ¥7, 90 min, scam-proof Install DiDi before arrival; English interface, regulated fares, digital receipt If taking licensed taxi, say 'da biao' (打表) before boarding; screenshot DiDi fare as reference Photograph the taxi license number from the rear windscreen on entering If you take the Maglev, transfer to Metro Line 2/7 at Longyang Road, not a taxi
scams.location: Pudong International Airport (PVG) arrivals hall, official taxi queue, Longyang Road Maglev terminus, Hongqiao Airport (SHA) secondary
scams.tldr: Black-market taxi touts at Pudong Airport intercept arriving tourists before the official queue, quoting ¥400–¥600 to central Shanghai versus the metered ¥180–¥220 — and the Longyang Road Maglev terminus runs a parallel version with higher tout density and tampered licensed cabs.

scams.name: Bund & People's Square Wine / Champagne Bar Overcharge
scams.description:
You are walking along the Bund promenade or a side street near Nanjing Road when a friendly, well-dressed young woman approaches in fluent English. She mentions a bar with a perfect sunset view of the Pudong skyline — "very local, my favorite place." The bar is real when you arrive: upper-floor, genuine view, stylish décor. The ambiance makes the setup entirely convincing.

She orders "just one drink." A bottle of champagne arrives. The bill delivered to the table is ¥6,000 to ¥20,000. Your companion has vanished. When you object, staff explain the per-glass, per-bottle, and private-lounge fees from a laminated card — and bouncers position themselves near the stairs. Credit-card chargeback is often the only recovery if the venue's posted menu differs from what was charged; cash and Alipay payments are much harder to dispute.

Choose your Bund bar yourself before you arrive and walk in without a stranger's introduction — M on the Bund, Bar Rouge, the Waldorf Astoria Long Bar, and the Peace Hotel Jazz Bar all have posted English menus and card payment with digital receipts. Any woman who approaches you on the Bund or Nanjing Road with a "sunset view" or "local favorite" invitation is working a role in this scam; respond with "bu yao xie xie" and keep moving.
scams.avoidance: Choose Bund-view bars yourself: M on the Bund, Bar Rouge, Hakkasan, Waldorf Long Bar, Peace Hotel Jazz Bar (all posted pricing, booking required) Walk past any stranger offering a 'local bar' invitation on the Bund Always verify a bar has posted English menu and card payment BEFORE ordering Pay with credit card for chargeback leverage; cash and Alipay are much harder to dispute If trapped, photograph the bill and inflated prices; dispute via card and report to 12315
scams.location: Bars near the Bund, Nanjing Road East/West side streets, People's Square north side, Xintiandi tourist-facing venues
scams.tldr: A well-dressed English-speaking woman near the Bund or Nanjing Road invites tourists to a "perfect local bar" with a Pudong skyline view, guides them to an upper-floor venue, orders champagne, then disappears when a ¥6,000–¥20,000 bill arrives with staff blocking the exit.

scams.name: Shanghai Tea Ceremony Ambush at Yuyuan & The Bund
scams.description:
You are near the Yu Garden bazaar entrance or the Bund promenade when someone approaches: "Hello, we are students — may we practice English with you?" or "Excuse me, could you help us take a photo?" The conversation is easy and the people are friendly. Within ten minutes a "nearby traditional tea ceremony" comes up — a chance to experience local culture, just around the corner.

The tea house is a short walk away on a side street or up an unmarked staircase. Tea is served and the experience feels authentic until the bill arrives: ¥800 to ¥2,500 per person. The "students" who guided you are no longer in the room. Staff show a laminated rate sheet breaking the cost into per-cup, per-pot, and ceremony fees. Police are historically unhelpful because you appeared to attend willingly; the practical remedies are credit-card chargeback and a report to 12315, China's consumer-protection line.

Any stranger at Yu Garden, the Bund, or People's Square who offers English conversation and suggests tea within the first ten minutes is running this scam — the "students" are professionals who work the tourist circuit daily. For authentic Shanghai tea, buy a Yu Garden entry ticket (¥40) and go directly to the Huxinting Teahouse on the pavilion in the middle of the garden pond, where tea is served at posted prices of ¥150–¥300 and no one will approach you outside.
scams.avoidance: Walk past any stranger at Yu Garden, Bund, or People's Square offering 'English practice' or 'photo help' For genuine tea at Yu Garden, visit Huxinting Teahouse (the pavilion in the middle of the pond, 1855) Published tea prices at Huxinting: ¥150–¥300 per person with clear menu Never follow a stranger to a 'nearby' tea house, even if they seem friendly Pay with credit card for chargeback leverage; report via 12315 and your card issuer
scams.location: Yu Garden (Yuyuan) bazaar area, the Bund promenade, People's Square south side, pedestrian shopping zones
scams.tldr: "English practice" students near Yu Garden and the Bund steer tourists to side-street tea houses within ten minutes of meeting, presenting bills of ¥800–¥2,500 for a ceremony the legitimate Huxinting Teahouse inside Yu Garden charges ¥150–¥300 for.

scams.name: Shanghai Disneyland 'Fast Pass' & Fake Ticket Scams
scams.description:
You plan a day at Shanghai Disneyland and look for tickets online or spot a seller near the Disney Resort Metro station. A third-party reseller offers "Disney Premier Access" fast-track passes at ¥800 per person — plausibly priced given the multiple official tiers. The Disney app's real Premier Access sells for ¥300–¥600 depending on demand, but the tiered structure of one-day, two-day, VIP tour, and Premier Access options is genuinely confusing and creates an opening for inflated or fake pricing.

You pay ¥800 per person. The seller delivers a QR-code ticket via WeChat or email that looks legitimate. You take Metro Line 11 to Disney Resort station and scan your code at the turnstile. The gate rejects it. The ticket is fake or expired. The seller is unreachable. Street touts outside the Metro station and hotel-lobby kiosk operators run this version most actively; genuine chargeback depends entirely on whether you paid with a credit card rather than cash or Alipay.

Book all Shanghai Disneyland tickets directly through the official app at shanghaidisneyresort.com before you leave your hotel — the app handles every ticket type, Premier Access, rider reservations, and dining in one place, making third-party sellers immediately unnecessary and suspicious. Do not buy from hotel-lobby touts, street vendors, or any platform not at the Disney URL. Pay by credit card for fraud protection if anything goes wrong.
scams.avoidance: Book directly via Shanghai Disneyland official app or shanghaidisneyresort.com Disney Premier Access is ¥300–¥600; anything higher is a markup or scam Shanghai Metro Line 11 to Disney Resort station: ¥5–¥7, 40 min, scam-proof Pay with credit card for fraud protection; avoid cash/Alipay for chargeback reasons For hotel stays, book only Disney Resort Hotel or Toy Story Hotel via Disney's own site
scams.location: Shanghai Disneyland main entrance (Pudong), Disney Resort Metro station, third-party resale sites, hotel-concierge packages
scams.tldr: Touts near the Disney Resort Metro station and third-party resellers sell fake Shanghai Disneyland QR-code tickets and inflated "Premier Access" passes at ¥700–¥800 per person — victims are denied entry at the gate with no recourse and no way to trace the seller.

scams.name: AP Xinyang Fake Market Bait-and-Switch
scams.description:
AP Xinyang Fashion Market below Science & Technology Museum Metro station and Han City in Jing'an are well-known replica goods markets that tourists visit openly. A vendor displays a convincing replica watch, bag, or accessory. You negotiate the price from ¥500 down to ¥200, inspect the item in your hands, and agree on the deal. The piece you have been holding looks and feels exactly as described.

The vendor offers to "wrap it properly" or "box it for you in the back." You hand back the item. What returns in the bag is a lower-grade version than the one you examined — same style, visibly inferior quality once you are outside. A variant uses a "diamond tester" or authenticity tool to prove a replica watch stone is genuine before the sale; the tester is rigged. By the time you open the packaging on the street, you are far from the stall and returning it becomes a confrontation with no resolution. Importing counterfeit goods is also prohibited in the US, UK, and EU; customs can confiscate them even for personal use.

Hold the specific item from inspection through payment and do not release it for "wrapping in back" under any circumstances — the switch happens in that window every time. Start negotiations at 10–15% of the first-quoted price and walk away if the vendor will not box the item in front of you. If you want legitimate shopping in Shanghai, Global Harbor, Xintiandi, and IFC Mall all have honest pricing and standard return policies.
scams.avoidance: Start negotiations at 10–15% of first-quoted price; walk away if vendor refuses Hold the specific item yourself from inspection through payment; refuse 'wrapping in back' Understand home-country customs prohibit commercial counterfeits; personal-use amounts vary but risks are real Consider alternatives: Global Harbor, Xintiandi, IFC Mall for genuine shopping with returns If shopping anyway, budget only what you can afford to lose entirely
scams.location: AP Xinyang Fashion Market (Science & Technology Museum metro), Han City Fashion & Accessories Plaza, various 'underground fake' markets
scams.tldr: Vendors at AP Xinyang fake market (Science & Technology Museum Metro) and Han City in Jing'an show tourists a genuine "grade A" replica during negotiation, then swap it for an inferior version while "wrapping it in back" — buyers discover the switch only after leaving the building.

scams.name: Pudong Airport SIM Card Tout Markup
scams.description:
You exit customs at Pudong International Airport and immediately need a working phone. A booth in the arrivals corridor or a man in casual dress approaches: "Tourist SIM card, 30GB, 30 days, ¥300." The price sounds reasonable for a month of data, and you cannot easily compare it on the spot. The official China Mobile and China Unicom counters are a short walk further into the same terminal, but the tout intercepts you before you reach them.

You pay ¥300 for a plan worth ¥100–¥150. In the better outcome the SIM works but you overpaid by 2–3x. In documented cases the SIM functions for seven days then stops — the tout is unreachable and the carrier will not service a third-party resale SIM. Passport information provided to an unofficial booth may also be collected without proper documentation or registration.

Buy an eSIM from Airalo, Holafly, or Nomad before you fly — a China 5GB 30-day plan costs US$15–US$30 and activates while you are still in the air , so you arrive with a working phone and no reason to approach any airport booth. If you want a physical SIM, walk past all non-branded booths in the arrivals hall and find the clearly labeled China Unicom or China Mobile counter in PVG Terminal 2 arrivals, where the official 30-day/30GB Trip SIM costs ¥100–¥150 with a carrier receipt.
scams.avoidance: Buy an eSIM before flying: Airalo, Holafly, or Nomad sells China 5GB 30-day at US$15–US$30 At PVG, use ONLY the official China Unicom or China Mobile counter — ¥100–¥150 for 30 days/30GB Ignore any SIM booth not clearly carrier-branded For short trips (<10 days), home-carrier roaming is often competitive Keep a receipt (fapiao) from whichever carrier you choose for any warranty or support needs
scams.location: Pudong Airport arrivals hall, along airport transit paths, hotel check-in desks offering 'tourist SIM' packages
scams.tldr: Unofficial SIM card touts at Pudong Airport arrivals hall quote ¥250–¥300 for 30-day tourist plans that China Mobile and China Unicom's official counters inside the same terminal sell for ¥100–¥150 — and in some cases the tout's SIM stops working within a week.
